stem: Why did Buffalo Bill's show succeed in the 1880s and 1890s?

stimulus.source_note: Buffalo Bill's Wild West poster, 1899 (Library of Congress, LCCN94513621). Public domain. Image viewed before writing.
stimulus.text: The poster advertises 'Buffalo Bill's Wild West and Congress of Rough Riders of the World,' 1899. At the right, Colonel W. F. Cody, 'Buffalo Bill,' sits on horseback, with the promise that he 'will appear at every performance.' The center shows 'Arab Horsemen' galloping and acrobats performing, and the banner at the bottom advertises 'the real Sons of the Soudan' and their feats of strength and horsemanship.

options.text: It taught audiences the census figures on western settlement
options.misconception: Background: the show sold spectacle, not statistics; the census figures belonged to Turner's essay.

options.text: It employed only Native performers and no cowboys
options.misconception: Background: the poster shows cowboys, Arab horsemen, and acrobats alongside Native performers; the cast was mixed by design.

options.text: It was funded by the federal government to promote western homesteading
options.misconception: Background: the show was Cody's private business; the government promoted settlement with land laws, not with circuses.

options.text: It gave audiences the thrilling, romantic West they imagined from dime novels

rationales.A: Background: the show sold spectacle, not statistics. The census figures belonged to Turner's essay.
rationales.B: Background: the poster shows cowboys, Arab horsemen, and acrobats alongside Native performers. The cast was mixed by design.
rationales.C: Background: the show was Cody's private business. The government promoted settlement with land laws, not with circuses.
rationales.D: Background: dime novels had already made millions familiar with cowboys and gunmen. Cody staged that same West live, with real riders and real sharpshooters, and the crowds came.
rationales.general:
Picture a reader who has spent years on Deadwood Dick, now watching real riders gallop past.
1. Ask what the reader already believes. The West is daring riders, gunmen, and narrow escapes.
2. Ask what Cody gives him. That same West, live, with horses, guns, and a hero on a white horse.
3. Name the success. A show that stages what the audience already dreams.
Remember: the surest hit is the story the crowd already knows, performed live.

figures.alt: A colorful 1899 show poster. At the right, Buffalo Bill Cody sits on a horse in a fringed jacket and wide hat. The center shows Arab horsemen galloping, acrobats, and riders performing tricks, under the title Buffalo Bill's Wild West and Congress of Rough Riders of the World.
